articles.title: RAM price hikes: the latest on the global memory shortage
articles.summary: RAM prices have spiked recently, growing by multiples as the data center boom sucks up supply from chipmakers.
articles.body: Random access memory, or RAM, is in just about every piece of technology we use. But it’s also the technology that AI companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta are using to power the servers in their massive data centers. Now, the world’s biggest memory makers — Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron — are taking advantage of a surge in demand, shifting their resources away from consumer-focused products and toward more lucrative deals with AI companies. The result is a severe shortage in RAM for consumer products, which is not only contributing to price hikes on the RAM kits used by PC builders but also for the manufacturers of a range of devices, including laptops, smartphones, gaming consoles, and a whole lot more. Some companies, like Raspberry Pi and Framework, have already raised the prices of their products as a result of the increase, while others, like Dell, Asus, Acer, Xiaomi, and Nothing, have warned about price hikes coming soon. It doesn’t look like the RAM shortage is going to subside anytime soon, as analysts at the International Data Corporation predict that it could “persist well into 2027.” Here’s all the latest news on the rising price of RAM.

articles.title: The Sonos Ace Ultra are the headphones Sonos should have made the first time
articles.summary: ﻿With better sound, better ANC, and Wi-Fi audio streaming, the Ace Ultra are finally worthy of the Sonos name.
articles.body: The original Sonos Ace headphones should have been a triumphant entry into a new product category. Instead, they were overshadowed by Sonos’s disastrous app redesign. And while the original Ace are well built, sound good, and are incredibly comfortable, they weren’t good Sonos headphones: Their flagship feature let you reroute audio from a Sonos soundbar to the Ace headphones so you could listen to your TV audio without disturbing anyone. But it was glitchy, and at launch it only worked with the $1,000 Arc soundbar, and only with one pair of Ace headphones at a time (Both of those have now been fixed). It also couldn’t connect to the rest of the Sonos system for music streaming. Now the Ace Ultra are here, at the same $449 release price as the Ace (which are now $349). They’ve improved on what the Ace did well, while finally adding the ability to pass audio from your Sonos system to the headphones and back (although it’s in “early access”). They’re what the Ace should have been the first time. [Product: Sonos Ace Ultra headphones | The Sonos Ace Ultra have the same clean, understated look of the original, which I appreciate. They’re incredibly comfortable for hours on end, even while I’m wearing my glasses, and though they’re ever so slightly heavier than the Ace — 0.69 pounds to 0.71 pounds with the Ace Ultra — that weight was never a problem. The ear cups are squishy and spacious, and like the Ace’s ear cups, they’re also magnetic and easily removable; Sonos sells extras for $39 a pair. The battery is also user replaceable (a kit costs $25), although a statement on the battery kit listing does warn that “swapping out the battery requires disassembly and tools, plus some time and patience.” The headphones also keep the tactile buttons and Content Key volume slider of the Ace instead of using capacitive buttons like the Sony XM series or Bose QuietComfort Ultra. I loved this setup and I’m glad Sonos kept the real buttons on the Ace Ultra. The Content Key reacts quickly and is easy to find while wearing the headphones. And its button functionality allows you to access the Sonos-specific features of TV audio swap and headphone linking. [Image: [Image: While the original Ace came with TV audio swap, that was the extent of their Sonos system integration. The Ace Ultra have rectified that, albeit with a caveat, by adding headphone linking. The headphones now show up in your system list, and with a press of the slider button, you can move your music from any Sonos speaker or speaker group — not just TV audio from the soundbar — to the headphones and vice versa. That includes audio coming into the Sonos system from a record player or CD player or anywhere else. Both TV audio swap and headphone linking use a Wi-Fi connection. It’s not flawless; sometimes I’d have to press the button a couple times to get the transfer to happen. If you pull the audio from your speakers to the headphones and decide to send it back later, it only goes to the closest speaker in your system, not whichever speaker or group was playing before. Adding it back to a speaker group has to be done in the Sonos app. The headphones also cannot be grouped with any speakers. I suppose the thinking is, if you’re listening to music on your headphones you don’t need it also playing from your speakers. One nice touch is that if you have different music playing on different speakers, pulling the music to the headphones from one doesn’t affect the rest of them. Headphone linking is in early access, according to Sonos, so it’s possible the experience will change. As Sonos’ own Wi-Fi vs. Bluetooth explainer points out, one of the main benefits of Wi-Fi audio streaming is that the higher bandwidth allows for hi-res and lossless audio. But right now, the Ace Ultra don’t take advantage of that. During the headphone linking early access period, audio over Wi-Fi with headphone linking is lossy. (Sonos has not said how long the early access period will last). Senior director of product management Andrew Sutherland told The Verge via email, “our focus right now is making sure the core experience is genuinely solid and reliable for listeners by using a high-quality, lossy-compressed stereo audio stream optimized for listening over WiFi. We’ve been really happy with the results. We’ll continue to build out its capabilities from there.” I appreciate the cautiousness in making sure headphone linking works properly, but it’s disappointing that Sonos shipped a product with one of its flagship features still in beta. [Image: There’s a magnetic pouch in the case to hold the included USB-C-to-USB-C and USB-C-to-3.5mm cables. At the moment, the Ace Ultra only support lossless audio over Bluetooth with aptX Lossless and a compatible device, or over USB-C. The wired USB-C or 3.5mm connection maxes out at 16-bit/48kHz, though, so there’s no high-res audio. There will surely be lots of debate on the forums about the tragic lack of high-res support, but the reality is most people won’t be missing anything. Newly designed 40mm drivers sound better than those on the original Ace, and an adaptive EQ makes real-time adjustments based on fit and any obstructions — such as glasses’ temples or earrings. The bass is richer without overpowering vocals, which is most evident in songs with a thumping low end, like Billie Eilish’s “Bad Guy” (one of my go-to bass tests). The kick drum through the verse and chorus has weight and drives the energy forward while the rhythmic bass line supports the voice. There’s also good stereo separation on “Killer Queen” by Queen with lead guitars to the left and right of the soundstage. I do wish the Ace Ultra had better midrange clarity, especially on busier tracks like Radiohead’s “The National Anthem” and its cacophonous middle section. The 8-band EQ Sonos added to the Ace Ultra (sorry original Ace owners, this isn’t for you) helps this a bit when I boosted the mids at 460Hz and 1kHz a little. While in there, I also added more high frequencies to open up the sound. With the tweaks, I got the Ace Ultra to a place where I enjoyed my listening across genres. It’s a good step forward from the original Ace, although I still prefer the Sony XM6’s default sound profile. [Image: Streaming music can be moved from a Sonos speaker to the headphones with a press of a button or through the Sonos app. The Ace Ultra’s active noise cancellation (ANC) is better than the Ace’s and now includes an adaptive version. It’s still not as strong as the ANC on the Sony XM6, Bose Ultra Headphones, or Apple AirPods Max 2 — it lets in more midrange and a few higher frequencies, as well — so if you’re mainly using them to block out ambient noise, those three options are better choices. But if you’re using ANC paired with music playing, the Ace Ultra perform well. Call quality is also better. When I was on a video call while my wife was having a phone conversation 20 feet behind me in the kitchen, the Ace Ultra kept her voice and other ambient noise quieted. They had a bit more trouble keeping out the noise when I went outside to a busy street — the Sony XM6 are much better at this — but I still sounded clear and easy to understand. Sonos has upped the battery life, from up to 30 hours on the Ace to up to 35 hours with the Ace Ultra. They come with the same felt-covered case with a magnetic removable pouch that stores the USB-C to USB-C and USB-C to 3.5mm cables. Sonos has taken a great first shot at headphones and followed up with an even better pair. They have improved sound, better ANC, and Sonos-specific features. And they’re one of the most comfortable pairs of headphones I’ve worn in a while. [Image: The Sonos Ace Ultra come in four colors — black, white, agave, and sand. But to get the most out of the Ace Ultra, you need to be an existing Sonos user, or be ready to spend hundreds more dollars. The cheapest Sonos soundbar that works with TV audio swap, the Ray, is still $219. And headphone linking is only useful if you have Sonos speakers. If you do have a Sonos soundbar and speakers and you’re looking for headphones, the Ace Ultra are an easy recommendation, especially over the original Ace — even though those are down to $350. If you’re not in the Sonos world, though, the Sony WH-1000XM6 (or even the older XM5) with their better ANC and sound quality for less money, are a better bet. Photography by John Higgins / The Verge

articles.title: The Unrivaled Atmosphere in End of Abyss Isn't Enough to Make This Survival Horror Metroidvania Worth the Ride - IGN Review
articles.summary: An unrivaled atmosphere isn't enough to make this metroidvania worth the ride.
articles.body:
The satisfaction of the metroidvania genre comes from a sensation of mastery – taking a place I'm unfamiliar with and slowly unraveling its complexities until I command dominance over its spaces and the threats that perpetually lurk within. For its debut game, End of Abyss, developer Section 9 Interactive tries to apply that format to an atmospheric horror adventure with twin-stick controls and instills a striking sense of dread inside a gargantuan labyrinthian facility. Its atmosphere only carries it so far, though; End of Abyss's exploration and combat slowly descend into a slog, and it never fully recovers from feeling like a routine procedure.

End of Abyss is centered around a young combat technician named Cel, who isn't given much in the way of personality. Cel is a silent observer who's trained to interact with the world through the scope of a gun. They skulk around this massive, desolate complex with only a few other soldiers four times their size, slowly attempting to discern what happened here. The place is abandoned, seemingly run by a series of AI boxes known as Security Control Units, which are trying to keep the facility from falling into total disarray. A mysterious voice calls out to Cel through these boxes, hoping they will help free this place from the zombified station workers who turned into enemy Husks.

Without much else explained, Cel is thrust into the cold concrete corridors and expected to survive. As I walked through dimly lit hallways and parasitic flea-infested tunnels, it was clear Section 9 was built of former Little Nightmares developers. The clay-doll aesthetic and isometric perspective is immediately recognizable. Atmosphere is the most captivating thing End of Abyss has to offer.

The grotesque detritus of vacant bedrooms litters the Habitation Sector, crafting a harrowing and bone-chilling opening section. I walked through every doorway with my thumb trembling on the right stick. Even with Cel's pistol drawn to keep my guard up, I was still terrified of what could be on the other side. The way a light flickers above an exit or how an enemy body encased in parasitic fungus is positioned all constantly feed into the uneasiness you want from a horror experience. These tricks work for the first few hours, but as End of Abyss dragged on, I began to see the seams of it all, and it eventually became too familiar.

What were once terrifying jump scares became predictable – corpses with important items conveniently placed in large open arenas consistently led to combat encounters I knew were coming. The supposedly dead enemies I used to fear waking up to chase me down always would, and thus it became routine to start shooting them before I even approached.

The mystery surrounding End of Abyss unsatisfyingly relied on the absence of information. Characters trade in vague uncertainties, often offering up little to no useful information about how or why we are in this facility. A few notes and documents are found scattered around its hallowed halls, but even slowly learning about what life was like here before our protagonist Cel touched down does little to actually paint a compelling picture. I pushed forward, turning on little AI boxes around this compound to activate an elevator, I searched for power cells to switch on a beacon, and I eventually descended into the dreaded lower levels to see what lurked below.

It wasn't until the back third of End of Abyss’ roughly 10-hour campaign that the plot started to gain momentum. The story suddenly took a front seat as characters began to explain the reason for our deadly trek through the compound. But because the buildup lacked tangible stakes, it was mystery for mystery's sake, and rarely did it feel of any consequence.

That's not to say that End of Abyss doesn't have its moments. Particularly in the last act when tiptoeing around the lower levels, I found note after note that brought me closer into the horrors of this world. Rooms filled with strange new oddities and remnants of experimentations piqued my curiosity and illustrated an underlying terror.

A few new weapons to add to my parasite killing arsenal also kept me invested in the search-action. Your options range from the Pulse Gun, a trusty and reliable pistol with unlimited ammo, to a flamethrower that lights up entire rooms in a wall of fire. The twin-stick shooter part of End of Abyss is no joke, either. Combat encounters can swing drastically if you roll the wrong way or get caught in a corner. I always felt in control of the situation even as I dipped and dodged through large hordes of enemies. So when I would slip up and lose that control, it became a struggle to regain my footing. That's where the combat thrives: walking on the razor's edge between confidence and hubris with a little uncertainty.

Enemy variety pushed me to do some experimentation in the action. Grenades were a staple in large group encounters, learning to manipulate aggressive enemy behavior to my advantage became a small game on its own, and grouping up mobs to maximize a red barrel explosion was a key tactic. More challenging enemies, like the long-necked Husk Latcher, made keeping a safe distance difficult; it perpetually charged forward and swung its long-reaching, claw-like head in my direction.

While I found the moment-to-moment combat mostly strong, the boss fights feel rote by comparison. Circular arenas with large creatures played out largely the same – roll away from the boss, pop a few shots into them, rinse and repeat. Some bosses, like the Centipede Husk, mixed things up a bit by leaving the arena and popping out of different corners to try and catch me off guard. Other fights are more focused on dumping large amounts of ammunition into the boss, and that's disappointing for a game with flashes of brilliance.

With the exception of the pistol, you'll need to manage your ammo and craft more at workbenches found around the different save points throughout the facility. Early on, managing my Riot Breaker shotgun ammo and choosing to save my limited supply for the moments that mattered felt reminiscent of other survival horror games like Resident Evil. However, after only a couple of hours, I rarely thought about my ammo counts, since the materials required to craft more bullets at a workbench felt like drops in a bucket. This trend continued as I acquired the Security Rifle – an armor-piercing long-range gun – and that minimized a potentially interesting dynamic.

Fragments are found around every corner, and they're a plentiful currency throughout. I found them on dead enemies, stashed away in lockers and treasure chests, and just laying in optional rooms. It was so abundant that I eventually felt nothing every time I saw that blue glow in the distance.

This resource problem began to seep into the cracks of the foundation and expose a larger problem: exploration is not truly rewarding. The interconnected hallways and twisting systems that make understanding how all of the locations fit together are part of the puzzle in a metroidvania. But here, the further I dove into the depths of it all, the more frustrating navigating this dilapidated station became. The lack of visual variety and identity across different areas made everything look the same, and it was difficult to pinpoint points of interest in an area to help anchor myself. End of Abyss became more about looking at the map every few seconds to ensure I wasn't going the wrong way than soaking in the foreboding atmosphere that surrounded me.

Unlocking shortcuts with keycards or opening a door from the opposite side didn't bring revelation or satisfaction. It often brought confusion about how or why these rooms were tied together and what use this shortcut would have. When every zone is the same gray-and-blue hue, it becomes a tired cycle to open up another cold steel door for the sake of it, or for a handful of Fragments I didn't really need. For every new weapon or piece of equipment I found, there were five rooms full of just Fragments.

And then there was the Containment Sector. This section of the map leaks radiation and would slowly tick away at my health if I stayed in the area. I quickly shifted gears and locked in, moving with surgical precision as I couldn't waste any time getting lost. Every few minutes my health would tick to zero, I would die, and I would respawn at a nearby checkpoint. It felt obvious that there was something I was missing, some sort of protection from the radiation, since the further into the sector I went, the stronger the radiation became.

Eventually I discovered a radiation suit mod that protected me from the constant damage. Instead of elation, all I felt was relief that I was done having to poke and prod random corners of this world for something that may or may not have existed. This entire scavenger hunt felt so detached from the Containment Sector and what I was trying to accomplish there, and it's a disconnect that even metroidvanias of yore didn't have.

Backtracking in End of Abyss is rough, even with a transit system that can take you to most zones. Cel does not move very quickly while sprinting, and the constant aimless roaming really pads out the overall runtime. These problems are exacerbated by multiple bugs that prevented me from progressing – random invisible walls that would stop me dead in my tracks on a ladder or prevent me from doubling back to a section I was just in. This caused me to have to restart at a previous checkpoint, losing 10-15 minutes of progress each time.

Despite the frustrations with exploration, the tone-setting audio design from Section 9 is some of the best I've heard recently. Pulsating reverberations of loud clangs and distorted gurgles rang through my headphones, sending shivers down my spine. The wet squelching of enemies as they scurried toward me made me want to crawl out of my skin. The audio gives End of Abyss a sense of scope that outsized its dark and tight corridors, making it feel like this facility goes far beyond the bounds of the screen.

articles.title: Marvel's Wolverine Ending Explained: How Insomniac Radically Changes Logan's Origin Story
articles.summary: Marvel's Wolverine offers a very different take on Logan's origin story and place in the Marvel Universe. Here's everything you need to know about the game's dramatic ending and how it sets up a sequel.
articles.body:
Marvel’s Wolverine is the first game since 2009’s X-Men Origins: Wolverine to revolve around the iconic mutant hero. And while that previous game was mostly an adaptation of the movie, this new one tells a completely original story set in the same universe as Insomniac’s Spider-Man games. Just like those Spider-Man games, Marvel’s Wolverine isn’t afraid to make some big alterations to the source material as its ambitious story plays out.

How exactly does the new Wolverine game end? How does it change what we know about Logan from the X-Men comics and movies? How does the game set up a sequel? Let’s break down what we learn and what the big questions are surrounding Marvel’s Wolverine 2.

A big part of Wolverine’s appeal as a character is that he’s an enigmatic bad boy with a mysterious past. Little by little, the X-Men comics have filled in the giant gaps in his memories, and the movies have mostly followed their example. But Marvel’s Wolverine is a little different. The game isn’t afraid to change up what we thought we knew about this character.

Over the course of the game, Logan slowly recovers lost memories and pieces together his murky past. Some of the revelations mirror what we know from the comics. His real name is James “Logan” Howlett. He’s been alive since the 1800s and has spent many decades wandering the globe, fighting in wars, and occasionally falling in love.

But beyond those basic details, Insomniac has altered a lot of the fundamentals of Wolverine’s past. For one thing, he doesn’t have any apparent ties to the Weapon X program or the shadowy figure Romulus in this universe. Instead, Wolverine seems to have acquired his adamantium skeleton from Apocalypse. At some point in the 19th century, Logan was recruited by Apocalypse to become the Horseman of Death (we’ll get more into what the Horsemen are in a bit). Apocalypse gave Logan his unbreakable metal claws and poured his dark will into his new servant, making him the ultimate killing machine.

Following that transformation, Wolverine came into conflict with the Japanese ninja cult known as The Hand. The Hand worship a demonic master known as The Beast. In the comics, The Beast is a real being, but in this universe it seems they’re actually worshipping Apocalypse. 100 years in the past. Logan was sent to slaughter The Hand, earning him the nickname “Shinigami” and the undying wrath of Lady Deathstrike.

At some point in the 20th Century, Logan finally broke free from Apocalypse’s influence and continued wandering the globe. However, that malevolent influence remains, and he’s fought a constant battle to prevent his dark side from consuming him ever since.

Marvel’s Wolverine chronicles what initially seems to be the first meeting between Logan and Jean Grey. In this universe, the X-Men don’t yet exist, and Jean is part of an underground group of mutants struggling to survive while enemies like Bolivar Trask plot their destruction. Logan and Jean first connect when they both attempt to rescue that group of mutants, and Logan finds himself immediately drawn to the woman he nicknames “Red.”

That setup in itself isn’t a huge change for the franchise. Plenty of incarnations of the X-Men mythos have focused on the mutual attraction between Jean and Logan, though usually Cyclops is there to serve as a rival for Jean’s affections. But the game makes a huge change to that lore by revealing that Logan and Jean are deeply intertwined and share a romantic history dating back many decades.

Essentially, the Wolverine and Jean Grey of the Insomniac universe are eternal lovers, not unlike Hawkman and Hawkgirl in the DC Universe. Logan himself is effectively immortal and unaging. Jean, meanwhile, has the power of the Phoenix and is constantly reincarnated after her death. Every time Jean dies and is reborn, she seems destined to reconnect with Logan.

The secret of Jean’s immortality seems to be her connection to the Phoenix Force. In the comics, the Phoenix is a powerful cosmic entity made of pure psionic energy. It embodies life, creation, and passion, and it’s deeply drawn to Jean. Bonding with the Phoenix amplifies Jean’s psychic powers to the nth degree, and it’s allowed her to cheat death on more than one occasion.

In some versions of the X-Men mythos (like 2006’s X-Men: The Last Stand), the Phoenix isn’t a separate entity, but simply a manifestation of Jean’s repressed dark side. It’s unclear what route Insomniac is taking with these games. But either way, the goal seems to be to present Jean as a force of life and creation, while Wolverine, as an agent of Apocalypse, embodies death and destruction. They’re forever linked, always drawn together but doomed to be torn apart.

In the absence of Professor X and his X-Men, Marvel’s Wolverine focuses instead on Nathaniel Essex. Essex fills that Xavier-shaped void in Logan’s life. He recruits our hero to join Team X, a strike force that includes fellow mutant killers like Mystique and Sabretooth. Essex even has his own remote mansion not unlike the Xavier School for Gifted Youngsters. His hope is to provide a safe haven for mutants in a world that hates and fears them.

But for anyone remotely familiar with Essex from other X-Men media (where he normally goes by the moniker Mister Sinister), it should come as no surprise that this character is nowhere near as benevolent as he seems. Essex’s goal is to awaken the millions of dormant mutants who exist across the globe, using an artifact called the Helix Device. That’s the same artifact that originally transformed Logan into Death, and it has a similarly nasty effect on anyone else who’s subjected to its Apocalypse-infused power.

The game eventually reveals that Essex himself isn’t a mutant. Rather, he’s spent the past several centuries harvesting mutant genes and implanting them in his own body, beginning with his poor wife. We also learn that Essex was responsible for Logan’s amnesia. He awakened Logan’s dark side, causing him to kill Jean, and then forced him to relive that act over and over again until Logan’s mind broke.

By the climax of the game, Essex’s heel turn is complete. He implants countless new mutant genes and dons his Mister Sinister armor. His goal is to unleash an army of Sentinels that will awaken the mutant race and make them slaves to his will. Fortunately, Wolverine and Jean manage to stop the Sentinels, and Logan battles his own mentor to the death.

But just before meeting his end, Essex blasts Logan with a concentrated dose of Helix energy. That fully reactivates the Shinigami within. Barely maintaining control over his bloodlust, Wolverine begs Jean to use her Phoenix power to burn all traces of Death out of his mind. Jean worries there will be nothing left of him in the aftermath, but Logan reminds her that he’ll still have her.

Jean does as requested. Unfortunately, that once again renders Logan an amnesiac. Death is gone, but so are all the memories Logan fought so hard to recover. Even his memories of Jean have been burnt away. As Jean reunites with her friends and works to begin rebuilding in the ruins of Madripoor’s Lowtown, Logan opts to leave and seek out the truth about his life. No sooner have these star-crossed lovers been reunited than they’re broken apart again.

Much like the Marvel’s Spider-Man games, Marvel’s Wolverine includes a few juicy tidbits for those who stick around after the credits and complete the endgame content. The game features a post-credits scene which reveals that Sabretooth survived his final battle with Wolverine in Madripoor. Victor is drawn to a remote temple by a mysterious voice in his head. That voice turns out to be Apocalypse himself.

Apocalypse makes it clear that he intends to recruit Sabretooth to be his new agent of destruction. As Death, Wolverine has run his course. But Apocalypse doesn’t want another Death. This time, he wants a War, and Sabretooth is just the man to carry that burden.

This scene makes it clear that Sabretooth will return in the sequel to Marvel’s Wolverine (whether that ultimately takes the form of Wolverine 2 or a full-fledged X-Men game). Expect the series to dig deeper into the Logan/Victor rivalry and the threat posed by Apocalypse.

A quick Marvel history lesson is in order. Apocalypse himself is one of Earth’s oldest and most powerful mutants. His already immense strength was augmented by Celestial technology, allowing him to manipulate his body’s mass and shape at will. But Apocalypse is usually accompanied by four Horsemen - Famine, Pestilence, War, and Death. Each of these Horsemen is a mutant Apocalypse has handpicked to serve as his emissary and transformed to become deadlier and more powerful. In the comics, numerous X-Men have served as Apocalypse’s Horsemen at one point or another, including Archangel, Gambit, and Wolverine himself.

The Insomniac universe is a bit different in that Apocalypse seems to focus on one Horseman at a time. For decades, he was content to turn Wolverine loose as Death and savor the blood that flowed. But now that Apocalypse seems prepared to emerge from his long slumber, he’s turned his attention to War. That seems like a very foreboding way to set the stage for the next Wolverine game.

In addition to that post-credits scene, Marvel’s Wolverine also saves one nugget for the very end. Players who complete all of the nightmare trials are treated to one last mission that unlocks a final memory for Logan.

This memory is set 75 years in the past. Jean, who now seems to recall her entire, centuries-long history with Logan, reveals that she once burned the Shinigami out of Logan’s mind to save him from Apocalypse. Despite losing his memories then, too, he pursued her across the world and throughout her many lives.

This memory is meant to be a comforting reminder that Logan has endured memory loss in the past, and that hasn’t stopped him from finding happiness with Jean again. This suggests that the two characters will again be drawn together in the sequel.

Though if we had to guess, it seems very likely that Insomniac will throw Cyclops into the mix to complicate the love affair between Jean and Logan. Perhaps Jean will encounter Scott Summers during her rebuilding efforts, with Scott being one of the many mutants awakened by Essex’s actions. In Logan’s absence, she may find new love from an unexpected source. Perhaps she’ll even be recruited into the X-Men by the time Logan tracks her down again.

Where Are Professor Xavier and the X-Men?

The most noteworthy thing about Insomniac’s Marvel Universe is that it has no X-Men. This world has a veteran Spider-Man, the Avengers, and even heroes like Daredevil and Doctor Strange, but no actual X-Men. For now, it has to make do with Wolverine and Team X.

So why aren’t the X-Men around yet? What is Charles Xavier up to if not pursuing his dream of peaceful human/mutant coexistence? We have to assume the culprit here is the relatively low mutant population in Insomniac’s Marvel Universe. Essex and his team are horrified to learn from Trask’s files that only about 10,000 mutants exist across the entire world, far short of the millions they were expecting. Instead, there are many people like Essex’s right-hand man Walter, those who carry a dormant mutant gene but display no powers.

It’s entirely possible that Xavier and/or some of our other favorite X-Men characters are part of that group. They may be blissfully unaware of their mutant heritage. If so, Essex’s Sentinel attacks may serve as a rude awakening for them. Even if a version of Charles Xavier with full psychic powers already exists in this world, it may not be until seeing the destruction in Japan that he fully recognizes the need for a team of mutant heroes.

Basically, Insomniac is building towards the X-Men, they just aren’t there yet. Based on files from a 2023 data leak , it would seem that the developer has plans for a full trilogy of games. Next up is a direct Marvel’s Wolverine sequel, followed by a full-fledged X-Men game. We don’t know how much those plans might have changed in the years since, but it seems safe to assume we’ll eventually see a proper team of X-Men in this universe. Based on how well Marvel’s Wolverine is selling , Sony will surely want to strike while the adamantium is hot.

Do you like the changes Insomniac made to Wolverine’s origin story? What are your theories about where the sequels are headed? Let us know what you think in the comments.

Jesse is a mild-mannered staff writer for IGN. Allow him to lend a machete to your intellectual thicket by following @jschedeen on BlueSky .

articles.title: 'This Is Your Dreamcast Moment' — Former PlayStation Boss Offers New Xbox CEO Some Words of Advice
articles.summary: Former PlayStation boss Shawn Layden has offered new Xbox CEO some words of advice as she resets Microsoft’s gaming business: “pick a lane.”
articles.body:
Former PlayStation boss Shawn Layden has offered new Xbox CEO some words of advice as she resets Microsoft’s gaming business: “pick a lane.”

In an interview with The Expansion Pass , the former boss of Sony Interactive Entertainment America called the decision Asha Sharma now faces Xbox’s “Dreamcast moment.”

This is a reference to Sega’s earth-shattering exit from the console business following the commercial failure of the Dreamcast. That call, made early 2001, ended a run of console manufacturing that included the likes of the Sega Genesis, Game Gear, and Sega Saturn. Sega instead focused on releasing video games on previously rival consoles, such as Sony's PS2.

Fast forward 25 years, and Xbox is in the middle of a dramatic restructure that has already seen nearly 2,000 staff lose their jobs , multiple studios either exit Xbox or face closure , and various games canceled . Xbox is now focused on fewer, bigger video game franchises such as The Elder Scrolls, Fallout, and Minecraft, with the likes of Halo moved over to Call of Duty company Activision . Through it all, there are question marks hanging over the viability of Xbox’s confirmed next-gen console, Project Helix.

With this in mind, Layden was asked if he had any advice for Sharma, having led a video game business of his own. He presented two options: go hard on taking on PlayStation now and in the future, with the assumed launch of Project Helix and PlayStation 6, or pack up those console plans and focus on software.

“You got to pick a lane,” he began. “Either you're going to be a platform competitive with PlayStation — which Xbox has not been competitive with PlayStation for years — but that's not out of the window. You know, you can still make another run at it. And there are certain decisions you have to make around that about the platform. We talked about exclusivity. We talked about, how do you incentivize third-parties to support your platform in a meaningful way? This is all things around the platform business.

“Or you sit back and realize you are the biggest game publisher in the world. Well maybe Tencent’s bigger, but in the Western world you are the biggest game publisher out there with Activision and Blizzard and Bethesda and all the other pieces. Be that. This is your Dreamcast moment, when Sega decided we're just going to be on PS2 and we're going to get out of the hardware business and just be a great software company. It can be done. It's been done before. So, that's my advice. Pick a lane.”

Microsoft has for years now fended off questions over whether it plans to exit the console hardware business amid poor sales of Xbox Series X and S and, before it, Xbox One. Publicly, Microsoft boss Satya Nadella and Asha Sharma have remained committed to console hardware, with Sharma saying it’s central to the company’s gaming plans. But Sharma has also said in recent months that Microsoft needs to think carefully about how Xbox consoles work and make money, particularly with the RAMpocalypse driving up prices.

In June, Sharma said the spiralling cost of new and existing consoles would require "radically different business models" over the coming generation . Speaking to Fortune , Sharma acknowledged the increasing price of existing hardware and components — fuelled by global crises and the rise of AI — and said the industry had "reached a point where it will be hard to imagine" mass audiences still being able to afford "thousands of dollars" for a new console generation.

And just this week, former PlayStation executive Shuhei Yoshida said Sony and Nintendo needed to make their current consoles last as long as possible amid soaring costs that have already prompted PS5 and Switch 2 price rises.

Big questions remain. What, exactly, does Project Helix look like? How far down the exclusivity road will Xbox go? And here’s the biggest of all: will Xbox eventually exit the console business?

Photographer: Patrick T. Fallon/Bloomberg via Getty Images.

Wesley is Director, News at IGN. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

articles.title: The Best, Worst, and Weirdest Star Wars Prequel Trilogy Games
articles.summary: There were more games released during Star Wars' prequel era than you can shake a lightsaber at, and while some of them were good, many were bad or really quite weird.
articles.body:
Star Wars: Galactic Racer might be set in the New Republic era, but podracing screams “Star Wars Prequels” louder than Pepsi, and the bloodsport is largely beloved thanks to a video game.

The saga is no stranger to incredible games, but titles based on Episodes I, II, and III get lost easily among the KOTORs and TIE Fighters of the galaxy. The Prequel Trilogy has earned a second look from fans after Star Wars’ modern decade of disaster, and developers are starting to be at least Clone-curious with bangers like Zero Company .

The Prequels may have more motion than we thought, and it’s worth a trip back to BBY to explore their gaming past. Where can Star Wars games go from Galactic Racer onward, and what should be left behind like Anakin’s mom?

These are the best, worst, and weirdest Star Wars prequel trilogy games. We’ve got shooters, racers, and ecology simulators all on deck, so let’s start with the straight adaptations of the films:

The flagship game for Star Wars Episode I: The Phantom Menace released alongside the film in 1999. Like most Phantom Menace merch at the turn of the millennium, the game was a commercial success for PC and PlayStation, but that’s more indicative of the massive Star Wars Prequel hype than quality. They sold a lot of Jar Jar Binks lollipops too.

The game recreates the film from its opening tea service to the Battle of Naboo, controlling a veritable Mount Rushmore of beloved protagonists in Obi-Wan Kenobi, Qui-Gon Jinn, Padmé Amidala, and Captain Quarsh Panaka, all voiced by rather dubious soundalikes.

Fate is a big theme through the Prequel Trilogy, the idea that one’s destiny is fixed and uncontrollable. The same could be said of the camera in the Episode I game. Pinned high above your character, the POV renders gameplay extremely unpleasant as you leisurely lob blaster bolts back at battle droids. You can embrace the dark side and cut down innocent civilians who side-eye your rat-tail as you push boxes and complete fetch quests in a garish Otoh Gungah, but you won’t find it fun for long.

Jedi Power Battles is the superior game. Released a year later on PlayStation and Dreamcast, it follows Episode I’s entire plot in order, but only to the extent that Turtles in Time is invested in the story of Shredder stealing the Statue of Liberty. We’re in beat-’em-up territory, complete with a handful of fighters, combos and minigames, and a few fun secrets.

It’s far from the best example of the genre, but if you simply need to experience the plot of The Phantom Menace and you’ve had your fill of haggling and handmaiden intrigue, Power Battles is the answer.

There aren’t really many options for Episode II: Attack of the Clones. Scenes like the Geonisian arena and its kaizo platformer droid factory seemed tailor-made for games, but the starcrossed tale only received one proper adaptation: a ponderous sidescroller on the Game Boy Advance which fails to capture the burning passion of the film’s love story.

Episode III: Revenge of the Sith: the Movie : the Game fared much better. A hack-and-slash romp through 17 stages, it’s a bit like Power Battles with a bigger budget and some basic XP upgrades. It’s packed with unlockable characters and noncanonical missions where Anakin unalives everybody and seizes control of the galaxy. For a film that lives and dies by its duels, the single-player boss fights and PvP combat don’t miss. Even the ubiquitous handheld ports were solid.

The Episode III game oozes a prestige package. Cutscenes completely spoiled the film which came out ten days later, though there are some crucial differences for gameplay purposes that kind of make more sense than the movie, like Anakin personally killing Mace Windu to cement his Dark Side heel turn.

EA’s Lord of the Rings: Return of the King has a similar vibe, and also spoiled the heck out of its trilogy-topping movie before anyone could see it. The games are alike in a lot of ways, though from our point of view we’d give the edge to Mordor over Mustafar.

Whatever happened to games like these? It turns out you don’t need full-motion-video or fancy motion capture to convey the essence of a cinematic story. Sometimes all you need is a little Danish plastic.

Traveller’s Tales began their decades-long dominance of the licensed kid’s-game space with Lego Star Wars , whose simple title doesn’t need to stipulate that it’s covering the Prequel stories, because that’s just what “Star Wars” was in 2005.

The Prequel era appears in numerous Lego entries, largely delivered through grunts and pantomime without an ounce of gravitas, and it works. The first Lego Star Wars, with 6.1 million copies sold, is easily the most commercially successful Prequel Trilogy game despite largely being a joke.

Star Wars movies are vehicles for drama, action, and special effects. The plots and characters aren’t really built with controllers in mind, and the best Prequel games do well to explore their margins in side stories.

Some of the more interesting titles of the era are prequels to the capital “P” Prequels, like the Xbox-exclusive Star Wars: Obi-Wan . Not to be confused with the disappointing Disney+ show, or Obi-Wan’s Adventures, the Game Boy Color game that might be a better use of your time than the nine-figure streaming series.

Ewan McGregor’s Obi-Wan makes for a great protagonist. He literally sits out the worst parts of The Phantom Menace in a spaceship, so you don’t really associate him with extensive haggling and child slavery, and Jar Jar Binks and the Gungans do not appear at all in his self-titled game. Instead, we explore young Kenobi’s journey from the mean streets of Coruscant to the fateful Neimoidian breakout room that kicks off the entire saga.

Originally planned for PC, with a unique control scheme where mouse gestures controlled a lightsaber, the game was personally kiboshed by George Lucas and reworked for the launch window of Microsoft’s console. The padawan’s green blade, aglow with emerald Xbox synergy, would instead answer to the analog stick of the mighty Duke.

The exploits of Obi-Wan are nice to have, but Star Wars: Bounty Hunter has a lot more to explain. Released shortly after Attack of the Clones in 2002 and set years before Jango Fett’s decapitation, it tells the story of how the simple man making his way in the universe was chosen to stand at stud for an army of armored doppelgangers.

You’re given access to Jango’s entire arsenal and a surprising amount of freedom, blasting through seedy underbellies with a jetpack and roasting civilians and bounty targets alike. Industrial Light and Magic and Skywalker Sound all worked directly with LucasArts for the first time to create the game’s cutscenes, with great performances from the movies’ Temuera Morrison, plus Clancy Brown as a rival Mandalorian bounty hunter who is no longer compatible with canon.

The story explores the unsavory side of Star Wars, the dirty, dangerous places far from the Force where crime lords rule with a cortosis fist and a guy like Jango fits right in. Bounty Hunter was cited as an inspiration for the doomed “1313” project, and you don’t have to squint too hard to see shades of Andor, either.

Films convey character much differently than video games, a medium where Kyle Katarn and Cal Kestis carry more clout than Luke and Leia. Star Wars games are great at focusing on characters that the movies don’t have time for. The foxholes of a galactic war are filled with Iden Versios.

Begun in Episode II, the Clone Wars were, a brutal conflict that rages across 400 billion stars and largely takes place off screen. Wrapped up tidily in Episode III, the Clone Wars created a huge void that expanded media was well fit to fill.

Released in 2002 for PS2 and GameCube, “ Star Wars: The Clone Wars ” waged the opening salvos from behind the wheel. Developer Pandemic used the vehicular combat game as a testing ground for the in-house Zero engine that would usher in the era of Battlefront and its many Prequel Trilogy trappings.

A GBA game, New Droid Army , emerged around the same time, while the amusing Age of Empires reskin Galactic Battlegrounds rolled out a Clone Campaigns DLC that let you lead the fight against space tariffs by playing as the evil Separatists.

These titles barely scratched the limitless possibilities offered by a war fought over trade routes between clones and robots. An animated series or two was in order.

Genndy Tartakovsky's god-tier Clone Wars microseries made the fight look actually cool for the first time, but its only interactive representation came as a Flash-based browser game. Dave Filoni, the ascended fan who now essentially runs Lucasfilm, cut his teeth on his own Clone Wars series in 2008, and this one made the leap from Cartoon Network to consoles.

Republic Heroes is a bog-standard platformer, while Jedi Alliance takes advantage of the DS’s stylus swiping for its dual-character lightsaber skirmishes. Both games meet the standard of “whelming” one might expect from a spinoff to a spinoff, but they’re overshadowed by “ The Clone Wars: Lightsaber Duels ,” the game every single person imagined the first time they held a Wii Remote.

The plot takes a back seat to motion-control action, de-emphasizing the outsourced assassination and turgid love affair that defines the film. Instead, it zeroes in on one memorable aspect of the movies for a fun and satisfying power fantasy as a vertical slice of the saga.

Lore is great. Expanded Universes are beloved for a reason. There are thousands of well-worn paperbacks yellowing in the Legends library that can attest to that, but too much lore can elbow out the cinematic impact that made Star Wars a phenomenon. What is “Star Wars” if not a series of archetypical characters engaged in blockbuster setpieces, any one of which could be separated from the whole as a standalone experience?

The trench run, the Battle of Hoth, Teras Kasi kombat… You can carve out any given ten minutes from a Star Wars movie and probably find a decent game in there. “Spaceship combat” was the first place anyone looked, which quickly evolved into a sub-line of respectable flight sims and shooters.

1998’s Rogue Squadron was an Original Trilogy affair, but the devs at Factor 5 included a secret that evaded even GameShark detection for seven months. The UK release of The Phantom Menace was celebrated by revealing the Naboo Starfighter that was hidden in the code. A gleaming art deco Buck Rogers ship that mogged the busted-up Y-wings in the Rebel hangar, the Starfighter made it clear that the future was here, and it was all about the past.

Battle for Naboo is Rogue Squadron with a Prequel coat of paint. Like its predecessor, it’s a mission-based series of skirmishes that makes the most of the N64 Expansion Pak, with a propulsive plot powered by dialogue and dogfights.

The Starfighter itself is back, with a little less aura now that we’ve seen a nine-year-old boy master it in seconds, along with a fleet of the finest ships the Royal Security Forces have to offer. Unlike other games in the series, you play as RSF Lieutenant Gavyn Sykes throughout the whole story. Cool guy, but he’s no Wedge Antilles.

Battle for Naboo is exactly what you’d expect from Rogue Squadron: the Episode I version. The game is most notable for including concept art and an hour of developer’s audio commentary crammed into the N64 cartridge. It was especially impressive in 2001, when DVDs spoiled us with treats and bonus features. We at IGN were sure it was going to be the beginning of a major development trend to come. You can’t always get it right for 30 years.

Factor 5 took their talents back to the OT for the GameCube’s twin Rogue Squadrons, but LucasArts didn’t leave the Prequel age behind.

2001’s Starfighter , the series PS2 debut, is no slouch. Less Star Fox than Ace Combat, the game mixes sim and arcade as it weaves through the narrative of Episode I from the perspective of three characters, including fan favorite Nym, a mononomic space pirate who would one day earn an 18,000 word Wookiepedia article.

Nym and his signature ship, Havoc, would return the next year in Jedi Starfighter , scrapping with Separatists in the antebellum of the Clone Wars. It’s a fuller package than its predecessor, but both rate highly among Prequel games.

For all its faults, the Prequel Trilogy always excelled when it came to space and aerial action, full of big battles between cool looking ships that sound awesome. Now this is podracing!

Actually, this is podracing: Thanks to George Lucas’s lifelong fascination with fast cars, so much of Star Wars is propelled by the energy of a showstopping death race, a promise fully realized in the Phantom Menace.

The film’s entire second act revolves around the Boonta Eve Classic, a 500 mile-an-hour grand prix through the twisted canyons of Tatooine. For the competitors, ILM dreamed up enough pilots to fill a Glup Shitto graveyard, most of whom die horribly while Greg Proops cracks wise. Star Wars: Episode I Racer dares to ask: What’s their story?

The 1999 game for N64 and PC features 23 playable pods, nearly all doomed to expire on Boonta Eve.

We embody racer Ratts Tyerell, family man, racking up wins and wupiupi in the months before he’s vaporized. We become Ben Quadinaros as he purchases pit droids and upgrades his extremely dangerous ride so it doesn’t fail when he needs it most. We are Anakin, forced against our will to endure Watto’s gurgling as we dream of freedom on the track.

There’s little combat in the game for technical reasons, and while it diminishes the chariot race tension of the movie, it’s still a standout racer on a system that had a lot of them.

A code allowed you to dual wield two N64 controllers, analog sticks akimbo as you cranked the engines yanking you toward victory or oblivion. It almost felt like the real thing. The arcade game basically was the real thing.

SEGA created several Star Wars cabinets with interesting hardware, but nothing ever let you enter the world of Star Wars butt-first like Star Wars: Racer. Plop into Ani’s plexiglass pod, place your hands on the throttles and pray the Force is with you. All that’s missing is the plasma coupler.

The well-received console game was followed in 2002 by a more aggro sequel, Racer Revenge . With an emphasis on interpod violence, it’s a more fleshed-out game mechanically that never quite took off, a possible casualty of the Prequel backlash.

Criticism was calcifying into consensus and fans had fallen out of love with the pastime of podracing. It would take two decades for another game to pick up the torch, first with the VR title Beyond Victory , followed by Galactic Racer, which proudly features the sport and its foremost ambassadors among several modes of roguelike run-based racing.

Pods aren’t the only way to burn rubber in the Star Wars galaxy. You’ve got ships, speeders, swoops, and, in 2001, super-deformed mascots.

Super Bombad Racing is the first and thus far only Star Wars kart racer. The physics are floaty and fun, and the chibified characters are cute. It won’t unseat Mario, Sonic, or Garfield as kings of kart canon, but it’s unique and almost charming at times, which is more than you can say for a lot of the games we’ve talked about so far.

With its jaw-dropping Dinotopia aesthetics and dialogue no sentient being would ever speak, the Prequel Trilogy is George Lucas’s own Death Stranding: the brazen self-belief of an artist with a budget and no one around to say no. Star Wars has been pretty buttoned-up as a brand ever since the Holiday Special, and with Disney at the reins we’re unlikely to see anything as wild as Episodes I, II, and III again.

The games they inspired looked and sounded the part, but rarely matched the unfiltered ingenuity of the films. There are a lot of platformers and third-person action adventures on this list, and even awesome racers and dogfight sims are pretty par for the Star Wars course, but a few titles tried something different.

Lucas founded LucasLearning in 1996, riding the CD-ROM edutainment wave that brought Number Munchers and Incredible Machines to middle school computer labs around the world.

The imprint released several Star Wars Prequel games designed to fit in school curricula, betting on the children’s love of Jar Jar Binks to teach them about fractions and natural science.

Star Wars: The Gungan Frontier sees the titular species in crisis: their bubble cities are overpopulated, they’re surrounded by giant sea monsters, and half the planet can’t stand them.

Boss Nass enlists your aid in colonizing the moon, manipulating its barren ecosystem for imported Naboo flora and fauna in a simplified Sim Life with hints of Spore. Planting trees and balancing the food chain while vibing to the ambient soundtrack is such a pastoral, zen experience that you almost forget that you’re assisting an invasive, extremely annoying species.

Anakin’s Speedway offers kids ages four and up the opportunity to help the enslaved child build tracks for racers to die on, while Pit Droids makes use of the adorable automatons as Lemmings-style problem-solvers, guiding them through mechanical puzzles that teach basic logic and spatial reasoning skills.

The quirky little cluster of learning games are a breath of fresh air after traversing Theed for the thirtieth time, but they didn’t exactly revolutionize early childhood education. If you’re curious how the whole edutainment venture panned out, the last game LucasLearning developed was Super Bombad Racing, which most would agree has little pedagogical value to speak of. The division folded in 2001, ceding the market shortly before the entire space imploded amid widespread internet adoption.

Games have always been quick to chase trends, even the ones based on movies that bucked them at the expense of good taste and narrative coherence. Flash games were in their heyday in the 2000s, and Star Wars embraced the Macromedia madness of it all with a clutch of Prequel-era games for Cartoon Network. More impressive was the expansive browser-based MMO called Clone Wars Adventures that boasted 10 million registered players before it folded in 2014.

Nothing chased a trend harder than Kinect, the much-maligned Microsoft peripheral that jumped on the motion control bandwagon by tracking your body movement with a creepy camera. Kinect Star Wars on the Xbox 360 might be its most infamous title.

The 2012 release is built on the Prequel Trilogy, at least as much as a grab bag of gimmicky minigames can be built on anything. There’s an obligatory podracing mode where you grip a pair of throttles that don’t exist, while the story campaign thrusts you into war as a Padawan of your own design, using the Kinect to control a lightsaber with flailing limbs in a quite uncivilized fashion.

The lasting legacy of Star Wars Kinect, however, has little to do with the Prequels. The Galactic Dance Off is a Just Dance-inspired collection of Now That’s What I Call Music hits repurposed for Star Wars, with parody lyrics that make one yearn for the subtle wit of “Weird Al” Yankovic.

Hollaback Girl becomes Hologram Girl, La Roux’s Bulletproof is Blasterproof, and Jason Derulo's triumphant ode to self-reliance is repurposed as “Han Solo,” spun by DJ Lobot while the titular rogue leads his dance crew of fascist collaborators in moves like “the Trash Compactor.” Even in the weirdest and most embarrassing Prequel game, the Original Trilogy still takes precedence.

LucasArts went down dancing. Kinect Star Wars would be the last game from the legendary studio before Disney moved development out of house, an ignominious end to an uneven era for Star Wars games.

Most of what we’ve discussed so far has been bad to mid at best, with a few standouts brushing against the ceiling of “pretty good.” We wish that we could just wish away our feelings, but it's true: for whatever reason, it’s hard to mine genuine excellence from the Prequel setting. Only a few games have.

Half the video game industry is built by gruff sci-fi people in faceless helmets. Master Chief, Doom Guy, Samus, and more all excel as blank slates on which the player can project. And what slate is blankier than a disposable clone?

In Star Wars: Republic Commando , released in 2005 for the PC and Xbox and set between episodes II and III, you are Boss, the gruff Clone commander of Delta Squad. Despite their genetically identical nature, his subordinates Fixer, Scorch, and Sev have fully-realized personalities all their own, like color-coded Kaminoan Ninja Turtles who obey every order from your contextual squad command button.

Your comrades are so well-written throughout the gritty, violent story that you forget they’re artificial drones at all, and you stop questioning why they have different voice actors despite their larynxes coming from the same vat. The team earned a devoted fan following, their own action figures and spin-off novels, and were clearly homaged by Dave Filoni’s Bad Batch in the Clone Wars cartoon.

Republic Commando’s first-person combat, with an always-appreciated diegetic helmet HUD, gives an infantry grunt’s perspective on the cosmic clash. It’s a more gory affair than typical Star Wars, and that’s saying something for a franchise with so many routine dismemberments. It eschews the esoteric mysticism of the Sith and Jedi and explores the unsung heroes whose blood oils the gears of galactic war like Andor would 17 years later.

Despite being one of the best Star Wars games period, let alone from the Prequel era, Republic Commando never earned a sequel, which means we may never learn the fate of the Clone we left behind. It’s rarely a good idea to get attached to characters when there’s a war on, especially if you’re playing Zero Company .

The turn-based tactical game from ex-Firaxis XCOM vets retains its spiritual forebear’s insistence that anyone can die when the odds aren’t in your favor, and if you opt into permadeath as the devs recommend you’ll find yourself mourning your beloved operators through the many hours of base banter and trauma bonding that make up the lengthy campaign.

Zero Company is, by all accounts, a big success. It’s got the highest Metacritic score for a Star Wars game in 22 years, and fans seem perfectly aligned on its awesomeness. Between Zero Company and the goodwill from Galactic Racer, no one is arguing over whether the Prequels suck. We didn’t roll our eyes at another Prequel game or use it to relitigate feature-length film reviews by cranky Wisconsinites. When it comes to video games, we’re ready to fall in love with the Prequel era all over again, or at least the best parts of it.

Charlie "Moose" Lopresto graduated law school, passed the bar, and made a financially questionable decision to write about games and movies instead. Contributing to IGN since 2021, he collects solo board games and transforming robots.

articles.title: Diablo 5 Game Director Promises a Return to Methodical Character Builds, but Players Don't Believe Him
articles.summary: Diablo 5 game director Joe Shely has suggested a return to more methodical gameplay.
articles.body:
Diablo 5 is still a couple of years away, but that hasn't stopped the speculation on how the game will actually play. People certainly expect a lot of elements from Diablo 3 and 4 to carry over to the new game, but Game Director Joe Shely has suggested a return to more methodical gameplay.

Seemingly in response to the video Path of Exile's Chris Wilson released about Diablo 5 , Shely took to Twitter where he promised "while Diablo 5 will continue to feature some DEX (moment-to-moment execution) mechanics, on balance the game will be an INT/STR game (planning and investment)."

While Diablo V will continue to feature some DEX (moment-to-moment execution) mechanics, on balance the game will be an INT/STR game (planning and investment). We are designing to the core tenet of ARPGs that any challenge can be overcome with the right build. — Joe Shely (@JoeShely) September 29, 2026

While Diablo V will continue to feature some DEX (moment-to-moment execution) mechanics, on balance the game will be an INT/STR game (planning and investment). We are designing to the core tenet of ARPGs that any challenge can be overcome with the right build.

There has been a lot of discussion around Blizzard invoking Diablo 2 when debuting Diablo 5 at Blizzcon , and how the team needs to shift away from the modern itemization and game design of the last few Diablo games to make that happen. According to Shely's post, it seems like Diablo 5 is heading in that direction. We'll just have to wait and see if Diablo 5's moment-to-moment gameplay is meaningfully different from Diablo 4's focus on infinitely scaling content that you clear in seconds. However, the community seems skeptical.

Over on Reddit, the top comment from user /u/Steve_Cage is simply "they said all this before 🤣🤣," and the top reply to that one is from /u/Tragedy_Boner who said "They ALL say this. And when the game comes out most people want to blast and not be methodical. No modern ARPG ever stays slow." Some people seem to think that even if this is the goal from the start, Blizzard will reverse course after launch. User /u/Usernameasteriks says "They won’t follow through, if they even try in the first place. Once the first wave of people complaining they can’t blast through content quickly they will restructure it all."

On Twitter, though, people seem a little more optimistic. User Dagon5 replied with "I'm happy to hear this. Honestly this is an opportunity to try the other direction from what D3/D4 was trying to accomplish. Just go all in on itemization depth etc, and skill systems." And that certainly seems like what Shely is setting out to accomplilsh.

I've personally never had a problem with Diablo 4's approach to itemization, and I like jumping in and seeing just how far I can push in the Pit each season. But, I also jump back to Diablo and Diablo 2 occasionally when I want to play something that focuses more on creative itemization. Luckily, even if Diablo 5 does lean towards Diablo 2's way of doing things, it sounds like the team will keep adding new seasons to Diablo 4 after launch , so you can always just stick with that game.

Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: Everything Coming to Netflix in October
articles.summary: Florence Pugh in East of Eden, Ben Affleck's Animals, and a hefty dose of comedy docs... all on Netflix.
articles.body:
It's officially Spooky Season, and Netflix has...gone a bit light on the spookies.

Sure, there's some choice Mike Flanagan with Ouija: Origin of Evil and the excellent Hush — plus movies like The Sixth Sense, Crimson Peak, Red Dragon, 2013's Evil Dead, three Psychos (you can skip 3 but don't sleep on 2), and even The Menu — but mostly October is about comedy documentaries!

From Norm Macdonald to Matthew Perry to Martin Mull to SCTV, it's all about looking at the careers — and, in some cases, demons — of those who've made us howl with laughter over the years. It's quite the cache! On top of that, there's a new East of Eden adaptation, a Victorious sequel series, the fourth season of The Diplomat, all the Bourne movies, and a new Ben Affleck film that's supposed to be nuts.

So while you ponder the how/why/who of Netflix raising its prices once again, here's a rundown of every series, special, movie, and doc landing on Netflix in October...

If you're just looking for a detailed list of everything coming to Netflix this month, you can jump to the full release schedule by day.

Mother-flippin' Florence Pugh and future Professor X Christopher Abbott star in this retelling of one of John Steinbeck's best novels, East of Eden. The most famous adaptation before this was the James Dean version from 1955 that was directed by Elia Kazan; granddaughter Zoe Kazan (Ruby Sparks) developed and wrote this new version, which focuses on the ongoing drama between two families — the Trasks and the Hamiltons.

Those who only know Martin Mull from his acting gigs (Roseanne, Clue, Arrested Development) will delight in learning that he was a massively popular virtuoso stand-up comedian in the '70s. This superstar spotlight was started by the late Bob Saget and eventually completed by Neil Berkeley after Saget's passing in 2022.

Mother-flippin' Josh Hartnett squares off against a mysterious sea creature in the new series Below . As a cynical, stubborn fisherman, Hartnett's Calvin must fight to protect his family, his community, and his vanishing way of life. Station Eleven's Mackenzie Davis and Stranger Things' Charlie Heaton also star.

Ben Affleck directs, co-writes, and stars in the new crime thriller Animals , about a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son gets kidnapped, forcing him and his wife (Kerry Washington) to go to extreme measures to get the ransom money. Steven Yeun, Gillian Anderson, and Ray Fisher co-star.

Victorious fans, rejoice! This spin-off/sequel focuses on Daniella Monet's Trina Vega (sister of Victoria Justice's Tori from the parent show) as her struggles to become an actress lead her back to Hollywood Arts, where she fills in as a substitute teacher. Plenty of past Victorious stars — except for Ariana Grande, naturally — will have guest spots, while Community's Yvette Nicole Brown returns as Principal Helen Dubois, a character that started over on Drake & Josh.

Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald - October 16

Directed by Judd Apatow, this closer look at the late Norm Macdonald is built from archival footage, personal photos, and rare home videos submitted by friends and fans. We're hoping there's a whole section about his epic 2008 performance at the Roast of Bob Saget. Look it up; it's worth the rabbit hole-ing.

Paralyzed by Hope: The Maria Bamford Story - October 23

Co-directed by Judd Apatow and Neil Berkeley, this exploration of reality-blurring comedian Maria Bamford is a must-watch that unpacks Bamford's mental health journey and her fearless comedy.

Also recommended is Bamford's groundbreaking two-season Netflix series, Lady Dynamite — a hilarious, surreal portrayal of her own attempts to rebuild her life after months of recovery for bipolar disorder.

The One About Matthew Perry - October 27

This three-part documentary series spotlights sitcom megastar Matthew Perry, including his tragic untimely death. Directed by Mary Robertson (Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV), The One About Matthew Perry features interviews with his close inner circle of friends as well as never-before-seen photos and videos from the Perry family's private collection.

SCTV: The Greatest Show You've Never Heard Of (doc) - October 30

With all six seasons of Canadian sketch comedy series SCTV now on Netflix, it's time for the uninitiated to find out all about this ensemble of comedy legends. Hailing from Toronto's Second City comedy troupe, SCTV was a late '70s/early '80s show that boasted the likes of Martin Short, Andrea Martin, Eugene Levy, John Candy, Catherine O'Hara, and Rick Moranis. Check out the full story of SCTV's influence on comedy and its lasting legacy, having launched a half-dozen or so comedy icons.

articles.title: Geoffrey Rush Has an Idea for How Barbossa Can Return in Pirates of the Caribbean 6
articles.summary: Pirates of the Caribbean actor Geoffrey Rush has said he's keen to make a return to Disney's swashbuckling franchise, if only to "annoy Jack Sparrow" one last time.
articles.body:
Pirates of the Caribbean actor Geoffrey Rush has said he's keen to make a return to Disney's swashbuckling franchise, if only to "annoy Jack Sparrow" one last time.

Rush is one of just three actors to appear in all five Pirates of the Caribbean movies, alongside Johnny Depp's Captain Jack Sparrow and Kevin McNally's loyal first mate Gibbs. And while we don't know yet which characters are set to return for Disney's long-awaited sixth blockbuster , all signs point to several classic characters being brought back.

Of course, Rush's character Hector Barbossa died in the finale of 2016's Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales, the franchise's final film to date. But even this would not necessarily stop him from returning, Rush believes.

Pirates of the Caribbean Movies in Order

"There's been a big enough break," Rush told Entertainment Weekly , discussing his desire to return. "I said, you know, I sacrificed myself for my daughter, I don't want it to be too easy and too cheesy that I come back and go: 'give me another payday.' I respect the scale of the opera that's almost been created in that 20 year period.

"I liken it to... Shakespeare," Rush continued, "and Hamlet's father coming back as a ghost. I thought, that would take good writing but just to come back and annoy Jack Sparrow for one more go. I'd even say, get the fans to write in what they'd like to see happen."

Back in August, Pirates of the Caribbean producer Jerry Bruckheimer said he was now talking with Depp about his own potential return to the franchise, despite previous comments by the actor that made such a return seem extremely unlikely , as Disney mulled other, alternative routes forward for the franchise. Depp's past legal issues with ex-wife Amber Heard saw Disney largely distance itself from the star, leading to some choice words from Depp in response .

Long-gestating plans have placed Barbie star Margot Robbie at the forefront of Pirates 6 if and when it does ever materialize. That said, Bruckheimer has previously confirmed his intent that "some" previous Pirates of the Caribbean actors would return for the next movie, while also offering "a new take" on the franchise overall. Depp, meanwhile, appears to have retained a strong affection for his role as Jack Sparrow , which is widely seen as his most popular character among his fans. Fellow Pirates star Orlando Bloom has strongly hinted he wants to see Depp back , as well. Could Rush also follow? Get writing those letters.
